name: Pulsed dye laser / V-beam for redness

lead: A pulsed dye laser (PDL), such as Candela's Vbeam, fades facial redness, visible capillaries (telangiectasia) and rosacea-related flushing by treating the blood vessels behind them. It has long been used for port-wine stains and other vascular birthmarks, and for some scars.

The laser emits yellow light, commonly at 595 nm, which hemoglobin absorbs. The energy heats and collapses small vessels while sparing the surrounding skin, a principle called selective photothermolysis described in 1981. The best-established published results concern birthmarks and scars; trials in facial telangiectasia exist but are few and small.

paras: It is performed by clinicians in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions spaced apart. Short pulses, adjustable pulse length and a cryogen spray that cools the skin surface protect the skin. Settings determine how much visible bruising follows, so some people choose gentler settings with less downtime and more sessions. Cost and number of sessions vary by clinic.

Reported effects include temporary redness, swelling and purpura (bruise-like marks), with pigment changes and scarring less common. It is a medical device used by clinicians, and results vary by condition.

web.title: Pulsed dye laser / V-beam for redness — Grokipedia

chain: Laser light absorbed by blood vessels
angle.text: Pulsed dye lasers such as the Vbeam fade facial redness, broken capillaries and rosacea flushing. The light is absorbed by blood in visible vessels, which collapse and fade, leaving a calmer, more even complexion. The technology is long established for birthmarks and vascular lesions; temporary bruising is common after treatment.

lead: A pulsed dye laser (PDL) is a medical laser that emits yellow light, commonly at 595 nm, which is strongly absorbed by oxyhemoglobin in blood vessels. The Vbeam family made by Candela Medical is the best-known branded line [1]. Clinicians use PDLs for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, facial and leg telangiectasias, rosacea-related redness and some scars [1][1].

The underlying principle, selective photothermolysis, was set out in a 1981 paper that modelled how wavelength, pulse duration and energy could be chosen to damage cutaneous microvessels while sparing the surrounding connective tissue and epidermis [2]. Flashlamp-pumped dye lasers were subsequently studied for port-wine stains [3] and for hypertrophic and keloid scars [4][5].

In appearance-focused communities the laser is discussed as an in-clinic option for persistent facial redness and visible capillaries. Published trials in facial telangiectasia are few and small; the best-established evidence concerns vascular birthmarks and scars.
infobox: Port-wine stains, telangiectasia, rosacea redness, scars

paras: Dye lasers use an organic dye as the lasing medium, which allows the wavelength to be tuned. In medicine the wavelength can be matched to a target such as hemoglobin or melanin, which limits damage to adjacent tissue [6].

Candela's Vbeam systems operate mainly at 595 nm and include a Dynamic Cooling Device that sprays cryogen on the skin around each pulse. Pulse durations are adjustable from under a millisecond to tens of milliseconds, and spot sizes of several millimetres are available [1]. Variable-pulse features are described by the manufacturer as a way to reduce purpura [1].

The 1981 selective photothermolysis paper proposed a model for choosing laser parameters to injure blood vessels preferentially [2]. A 1988 analysis examined how pulse duration and long-term therapy affected port-wine stain treatment with the pulsed dye laser [3]. Candela's account, as summarised by Grokipedia, dates its first pulsed dye laser to the 1980s, with Vbeam branded models following in the 2000s [1]. These manufacturer-linked dates have not been independently verified here.

Rosacea references describe laser and pulsed-dye approaches as mainly used to reduce visible telangiectasias by targeting hemoglobin [7]. A registered trial from China compared pulsed dye laser and intense pulsed light for facial telangiectasia in 150 participants [8]. Smaller registered pilots have examined PDL for telangiectasia in systemic scleroderma [9].

Port-wine stains are the classic indication, with comparisons of 577 nm and 595 nm wavelengths registered in trials [10]. A 1995 Lancet study treated sternotomy scars with a 585 nm flashlamp-pumped laser [4], and a randomised comparison against intralesional corticosteroid and 5-fluorouracil examined keloidal and hypertrophic scars [5]. Uses reported by the manufacturer also include acne, striae and psoriasis [1].

The published literature on pulsed dye lasers is largest for port-wine stains and scars [3][4][5][3]. For facial redness and telangiectasia, registered trials are small, including a 150-person comparison of PDL with intense pulsed light [8] and a 21-person scleroderma pilot [9]. Trials of PDL combined with other treatments for port-wine stain have also been registered [11]. No large randomised trial specifically in appearance-driven facial redness was identified here.

The cooling spray is described as lowering discomfort and surface injury [1]. Temporary purpura is the commonly described trade-off of pulsed dye lasers, and manufacturers market longer or multi-pulse modes as ways to limit it [1]. The rosacea literature notes that the technique aims to destroy vessels without rupturing them, which is the intent of the longer pulses [7]. The FDA has cleared Vbeam systems for a range of vascular and other indications, according to the manufacturer-linked summary [1].

The laser appears in appearance communities as a hardmaxxing option for persistent redness and broken capillaries, alongside topical redness products. Posts typically compare it with intense pulsed light and describe bruising and number of sessions as the main practical considerations. This wiki did not identify citable forum threads for this specific topic.
